    PROJECT NO. 58000                                      §      BEFORE THE
    RULEMAKING TO UPDATE WHOLESALE                         §      PUBLIC UTILITY
    AND IOU RETAIL TRANSMISSION COST                       §      COMMISSION
    RECOVERY IN THE ERCOT REGION                           §      OF TEXAS



COMMENTS OF ANTORA ENERGY

August 11, 2026

Antora Energy ("Antora") files these Comments in response to the Proposal for Publication
("PFP") in this rulemaking, and in accordance with the Public Utility Commission of Texas's
("Commission's") request for comments.

Antora respectfully submits these comments on the Proposal for Publication in Project No.
58000, approved for publication by the Commission on July 9, 2026, which would amend 16
TAC §25.192 and §25.193 and adopt new §25.252 to update wholesale and retail transmission
cost recovery in the ERCOT region.1,2 Antora's central theme in these comments is that cost
allocation should follow cost causation — and should reward, not penalize, load behavior that
measurably lowers transmission costs for all other customers. Antora supports changes that
allocate a fair share of costs to load and require cost pass throughs where a load’s firm
consumption increases network infrastructure costs. However, to avoid sending perverse
investment and operations signals the PUCT must design any minimum demand charge in a
manner that allows non-firm consumption to reduce system costs by using only low-value
generation, avoid or be curtailed during peaks and thereby avoid charges for transmission system
costs not caused by that load.

 I. Introduction and Interest of Antora Energy

Antora develops and operates thermal storage facilities that rapidly charge with low-cost,
off-peak electricity and deliver reliable industrial heat, industrial process steam, and power to
manufacturers and the grid. Flexibility is the design basis of the asset: electricity purchases from
the grid are decoupled from energy delivery. Antora achieves this by converting electricity into
heat stored in carbon blocks, doing so when excess electricity on the system allows for low-cost
charging. The energy can then be delivered in its thermal form to industrial customers, or
converted back to electricity. Because a facility charges flexibly rather than operating
continuously, it may have a relatively high contracted or nameplate demand but low load factor,
with very high flexibility and nearly instantaneous curtailability. Thermal storage projects for
industrial heat delivery have an annual load factor of approximately 30 percent.

Antora’s flexible industrial demand translates into real regional economic value: hundreds of
millions of dollars in new industrial investment, increased local tax revenue and jobs, support for
agricultural, biofuels production, and other industries that require process heat and cost
reductions for existing utility customers through better utilization of existing grid assets. Antora
has late stage developments in Texas including an interconnection filing in Batch Zero while
Antora has recently energized a project that would be classified as a Large Load within
Midcontinent Iso territory in Big Stone, South Dakota that operates under a coincident peak
based cost structure.

Transmission is sized for coincident peak demand, and peak therefore drives nearly all
incremental transmission investment.3 Highly flexible loads that can be curtailed as needed do
not contribute to peak transmission needs. Off-peak consumption uses existing spare capacity at
near-zero marginal cost. Because Antora's facilities are designed to avoid coincident peaks and
have low load factors, are price sensitive and highly flexible, they avoid coincident peaks, charge
only when the grid has spare capacity, and when low-value hours of generation are available.
That means Antora’s thermal storage projects “fill valleys” of demand and should not be
confused with additional on-peak load combined with low utilization of grid assets.

A load that verifiably avoids coincident peaks — and, under the alternative proposed in Section
IV below, is contractually barred from consuming at peak — adds no peak-driven transmission
investment, so planners can rely on peak avoidance rather than build for it. Antora’s projects are
different from other Demand Response or strategically peak avoidant loads that may decide peak

Highly flexible loads reduce generation curtailment by consuming in low-demand, high-supply
hours. Flexible-load charging concentrates in low-price hours, regularly absorbing energy that
would otherwise be curtailed — improving generator economics and the productivity of
transmission already built to move that energy. In 2024, grid congestion forced ERCOT to curtail
more than 8 terawatt-hours of wind and solar generation.4 Wind and solar together met 36
percent of ERCOT's electricity demand in the first nine months of 2025 and are ERCOT's
fastest-growing generation sources,5 making demand that can absorb curtailed output
increasingly valuable to the system. Furthermore, highly flexible loads can site within
export-constrained areas and consume energy that congestion or export limitations would
otherwise strand, reducing congestion and the pressure for congestion-driven upgrades.

Antora's projects typically exceed the 75 MW demand large-load-customer threshold under
proposed 16 TAC §25.1946 and, despite their system benefits, would be fully subject to the
proposed minimum billing demand ("MBD"), pre-energization billing, and class-allocator
substitution addressed in this rulemaking.

Antora supports Senate Bill 6's objectives of ensuring that large loads pay their fair share of
transmission costs and protecting residential and small commercial customers from cost shifts.7

II. Demand Charges Untethered from Coincident Peak Eliminate the Market Signal for
Flexibility

Under the PFP, the MBD equals the greater of (A) the customer’s contracted peak demand, (B)
its highest non-coincident peak (“NCP”) demand in the preceding year, or (C) its actual
coincident-peak demand; the MBD applies when capacity is available and for a period of no less
than 20 years.8 Billing commences at the level of available service, irrespective of whether the
large-load customer has energized or is fully using its available capacity.9

Collectively, these design features convert every flexible load into a firm load for billing purposes
on day one. This sends poor, inefficient investment signals and poor operation signals,
discouraging the beneficial load behaviors described in Section II that lower transmission costs
for everyone else while utilities will be forced to build transmission based on a contracted peak.
Without changes, the MBD risks eliminating the investment opportunity in Texas for large highly
flexible loads, like Antora’s thermal storage, that can reduce and share fairly allocated grid costs.


       1.​ Non-Coincident Peak Demand charges are a blunt instrument that destroys the
           value of flexibility. A load that pays the same transmission charge whether it consumes at
           system peak or only in the deepest off-peak valleys of demand has no remaining signal to
           curtail, shift, or respond transmission costs. The central economic case for building
           flexibility into a facility — storage, curtailment capability, price-responsive scheduling —
           is transmission cost causation and subsequent cost allocation. Charges on contracted or
           non-coincident demand substantially reduce or eliminate the rationale for investing in
           flexibility and encourage all customers to consume like a firm load. Overpricing off-peak
           network use deters investment in flexible loads that raise system utilization and steers
           investment toward full-firm configurations that increase total system costs — causing an
           unnecessarily overbuilt and expensive system.

           In Antora’s case the flexibility value destruction is even more severe: Antora’s industrial
           heat storage projects are designed to charge at ~3 times their discharge rate to maximize
           their ability to absorb low value hours of electricity generation and completely avoid high
           cost (and peak) hours. Under the MBD, that means a triple penalty for investment that

          supports grid stability, reduces curtailment and congestion and causes minimal or no grid
         infrastructure costs.
     2.​ MBD sends perverse operations signals: Further, the MBD not only sends poor
         investment signals, it harms sound system operations. Once flexibility earns them nothing
         (or even contributes to increased charges by concentrating consumption off peak), loads
         are much more likely to consume at peak. This will increase coincident peaks, increase
         capital costs and put additional pressure on the residential rates the rule is meant to
         protect.
     3.​ Non-coincident peak demand charges for curtailable customers sever cost causation.
         The premise of §25.192's coincident-peak allocation is that network transmission costs
         are driven by coincident peak demand. The MBD nonetheless charges a load for peak
         network capacity even where that load avoids any contribution to system peaks. Because
         a customer’s non-coincident peak, by definition, occurs when the system has spare
         capacity, billing NCP-based demand at rates comparable to coincident-peak rates charges
         customers for capacity their usage does not cause — a result that cannot be squared with
         standard cost-allocation principles.
     4.​ Non-coincident peak demand charges cross-subsidize peak consumption and
         perversely incentivize firm-load growth. If peak-driven costs are partly recovered from
         flexible loads that consume only off peak, consumption at peak is underpriced for firm
         loads. Again, by effectively subsidizing peak consumption, this accelerates the very
         peak-demand growth and transmission buildout the Commission seeks to manage — the
         opposite of the rule's intended outcome.
     5.​ Legal risk under Public Utilities Regulatory Authority

         and distribution rates remain fully cost-of-service regulated under PURA. The MBD

         unreasonably preferential, prejudicial, or discriminatory but must be sufficient, equitable,
         and consistent in application to each class of consumer.”10 Wholesale transmission rates
         under §25.192 are likewise Commission-set under PURA's transmission cost-recovery
         provisions.11 An MBD that compels flexible loads to pay for peak capacity they do not

III. Distinguishing Committed Industrial Flexibility

In sections IV and V below, we recommend limited alternatives to the MBD, should the
commission determine a coincident peak based charge is insufficient. The Section VI narrow
alternative and the Section VII hybrid proposal sorts loads by verifiable, enforceable
commitments rather than industry label — any load unwilling to accept binding curtailment pays
the default; eligibility is earned by performance, not granted by industry classification. In this
section we differentiate between certifiable highly flexible loads and load that may vary their
demand response behavior subject to economic conditions.

       1.​ Physical versus financial flexibility. Antora's flexibility is embedded in the asset:
           thermal storage decouples charging from delivery, so peak avoidance is the permanent
           design basis and can be committed contractually for the life of the facility. Antora's
           thermal storage is also designed for multi-day operation, allowing it to accept curtailment
           across extended periods of grid stress without interrupting service to its industrial hosts.
           This means nearly limitless flexibility to support grid reliability and lower grid costs,
           where economic demand response, unless tied to enforceable commitments, floats with
           opportunity costs — flexibility that cannot be committed and can evaporate when margins
           rise.
       2.​ Anchored, long-lived assets. Antora facilities are capital-intensive infrastructure serving
           long standing and fixed Texas industrial plants under long-term offtake contracts.
           Containerized mining loads can relocate to the next cheapest grid, which is precisely the
           stranded-infrastructure risk this rule targets.
       3.​ Wider economic development. Thermal storage loads directly support the Texas
           manufacturing and industrial base — jobs, local tax base, and onshoring of industrial
           capacity — rather than exporting a purely digital or financial product.
       4.​ Security and resilience for Texas industry. Stored energy provides firm, continuous
           heat and power to industrial hosts and the grid even while the electric load curtails during
           grid stress — the load steps off the grid when prices rise, including during peaks, instead
           of competing with residential customers, while Texas industry keeps running. Stable,
           low-cost industrial energy, and the resiliency of decoupling industrial supply from grid
           conditions, are competitiveness and security assets for the state.
       5.​ Reliability contribution. Committed flexible/curtailable loads function as dispatchable
           demand reduction during scarcity, complementing SB 6's emergency curtailment
           framework for large loads under PURA §37.056116 rather than straining it.

 IV. Alternative A: If Demand-Based Charges Are Retained, Provide Alternative for
Low-Load-Factor, Curtailable, Highly Flexible, Price-Responsive Loads

       1.​ Define highly flexible, curtailable load by behavior, not industry. Any large load
           customer should be billed and allocated on actual coincident-peak demand rather than the
           MBD, which would be comprised of firm + curtailable load, if it:
                a.​ operates as a low-load-factor, price-responsive load and accepts a binding, tariffed
                    curtailment obligation during coincident-peak-risk windows and ERCOT-declared
                    emergency conditions;
                b.​ provides real-time telemetry and settlement-quality metering (already required by
                    the PFP); and
                c.​ is automatically billed demand charge for any monthly period in which it fails to
                    perform (post commissioning and full energization) — a self-enforcing true-up
                    requiring no enforcement proceeding. In practice: if the facility fails to curtail, or
                    its load coincides with system peaks, it is billed the full demand charge for each
                    monthly period in which it fails to perform.
       2.​ Planning alignment. For flexible loads under this carve out, any portion of the customers
           demand that is firm should be either separately metered and treated like other loads, or
           identified as the customer's committed firm demand level to be entered into the ALLOC
           class allocator and ERCOT planning cases.
       3.​ Precedent within the PFP itself. The ALLOC definition's “unless otherwise ordered by
           the commission” clause shows the Commission already anticipates cases where MBD
           substitution is inappropriate.17 A standing, criteria-based carve-out is administratively
           superior to case-by-case relief.
       4.​ Not a loophole. The carve-out is earned by enforceable commitments and forfeited
           automatically on non-performance — a speculative load unwilling to bind to firm
           curtailment commitments pays the default MBD. It protects other ratepayers
           automatically, requires no Commission judgment about which industries are “worthy,”
           and complements SB 6's existing curtailment authority over large loads during
           emergencies under PURA §37.0561.18
       5.​ Should the Commission decide that a broader exclusion from the MBD is inappropriate,
           it should consider a narrower technology specific carve out. Thermal Energy Storage acts
           substantially similar to Electrical Energy Storage in charging from the grid during
           low-value hours. Wholesale storage load is exempt from demand charges per 16 TAC §

V. Alternative B: 85/15 Hybrid: Coincident Peak Demand Charge Plus Unavoidable
Volumetric Charge for All Large Customers

         Another alternative would charge all large loads for operational costs, without pushing
         capital costs driven by coincident peak onto loads that have no role in causing those
         costs:
     1.​ Design: recover 85% of the transmission revenue requirement allocated to large
         customers through coincident-peak demand charges, and 15% through an unavoidable
         volumetric ($/MWh) charge applied to all consumption by large customers. 22
     2.​ Directly answers the cost-shift concern that motivated the MBD: no large load can
         reduce its transmission contribution to zero — every MWh consumed contributes —
         addressing PUCT Staff's finding in the Project No. 58484 draft report that the current 4CP
         methodology allows some flexible large loads to reduce their transmission cost
         obligations without a commensurate reduction in the system costs they cause.23
     3.​ Preserves the efficiency signal: the 90% CP component retains a strong incentive to stay
         off coincident peaks, which is what avoids future transmission investment.
     4.​ Proportionality: low-load-factor flexible loads pay meaningfully in proportion to their
         actual use of the network; high-load-factor, always-on loads pay commensurately with
         their around-the-clock network use.
     5.​ Administrative simplicity: this hybrid approach would include two published rates; no
         customer-specific minimums, ratchets, 20-year terms, true-ups, or ALLOC substitutions;
         uniform treatment of all large customers regardless of industry.

VI. Conclusion and Requested Actions

Antora respectfully requests that the Commission base transmission billing and class allocation
on actual coincident-peak demand under whatever coincident-peak methodology the
Commission adopts. The Commission should reject demand charges based on contracted or
non-coincident demand.

If any demand-based minimum is retained, it should incorporate either the behavioral carve-out
set forth in Section V or the 90/10 hybrid recovery mechanism set forth in Section VI. If any
minimum is retained without such a carve-out, it should be aligned with phased energization
schedules, confined to NCP-driven direct-interconnection facilities, structured to exclude
minimum billing demand values from the ALLOC class allocator for verified flexible loads, and
shortened from its proposed 20-year term. Any residual or operations-and-maintenance-related
share of cost assigned to large loads should be recovered on an energy ($/MWh) basis rather than
an NCP basis, and demand served entirely within a private use network should be expressly
excluded from minimum billing demand, billing determinants, and class allocation. Antora offers
to provide operational data and to participate in any workshop or cost-benefit analysis the
Commission convenes on flexible-load transmission billing.


Respectfully submitted,

 EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Antora is a thermal energy storage developer whose facilities charge flexibly during off-peak
hours to deliver firm industrial heat and power; cost allocation that rewards this behavior lowers
costs for all ratepayers while supporting new industrial investment in Texas. Antora Energy
respectfully submits these comments on the Commission’s Proposal for Publication (“PFP”) in
Project No. 58000 to raise a targeted, remediable concern: as drafted, the proposed minimum
billing demand (“MBD”) charges flexible, curtailable large loads — including thermal energy
storage — for transmission capacity based on contracted or non-coincident peak demand, rather
than the coincident peak demand that actually drives transmission investment. That design
eliminates the price signal that rewards loads for consuming during off-peak, low-cost hours and
avoiding system peaks, and it does so precisely for facilities — like Antora’s — that are
engineered to fill demand valleys, absorb low value hours of generation that would otherwise be
curtailed, and impose little to no incremental transmission cost.

Antora requests that the Commission:

           1.​ Base transmission billing and class allocation on actual coincident-peak demand,
               consistent with the cost-causation principle underlying 16 TAC §25.192 and
               PURA Chapter 36;
           2.​ Reject demand charges keyed to contracted or non-coincident peak demand,
               which cross-subsidize peak consumption and eliminate the incentive for
               investment in flexible load;
           3.​ If a demand-based minimum is retained, adopt either (a) a behavioral alternative
               billing framework under which loads earn coincident-peak-only billing by
               accepting binding, tariffed curtailment obligations (Section III below), or (b) an
               85/15 hybrid recovery mechanism combining a coincident-peak demand charge
               with a small unavoidable volumetric charge (Section IV below);
                    a.​ Recover any residual, non-coincident-peak-driven cost share on an energy
                        ($/MWh) basis rather than a non-coincident-peak basis.

           4.​ Exclude load served entirely within a private use network from the MBD, billing
               determinants, and the ALLOC class allocator, since such load never uses the
               shared transmission network; and
           5.​ Recover any residual, non-coincident-peak-driven cost share on an energy
               ($/MWh) basis rather than a non-coincident-peak basis.

Antora offers to provide operational data and to participate in any workshop or cost-benefit
analysis the Commission convenes on flexible-load transmission billing.

Antora Energy ("Antora") files these Comments in response to the Proposal for Publication

Antora respectfully submits these comments on the Proposal for Publication in Project No.
58000, approved for publication by the Commission on July 9,2026, which would amend 16
TAC §25.192 and §25.193 and adopt new §25.252 to update wholesale and retail transmission
cost recovery in the ERCOT region.1,2 Antora's central theme in these comments is that cost
allocation should follow cost causation - and should reward, not penalize, load behavior that
measurably lowers transmission costs for all other customers. Antora supports changes that
allocate a fair share of costs to load and require cost pass throughs where a load's firm

 I. Introduction and Interest of Antora Energy

Antora develops and operates thermal storage facilities that rapidly charge with low-cost,
off-peak electricity and deliver reliable industrial heat, industrial process steam, and power to
manufacturers and the grid. Flexibility is the design basis of the asset: electricity purchases from
the grid are decoupled from energy delivery. Antora achieves this by converting electricity into
heat stored in carbon blocks, doing so when excess electricity on the system allows for low-cost
charging. The energy can then be delivered in its thermal form to industrial customers, or
converted back to electricity. Because a facility charges flexibly rather than operating
continuously, it may have a relatively high contracted or nameplate demand but low load factor,
with very high flexibility and nearly instantaneous curtailability. Thermal storage projects for
industrial heat delivery have an annual load factor of approximately 30 percent.

Antora's flexible industrial demand translates into real regional economic value: hundreds of
millions of dollars in new industrial investment, increased local tax revenue and jobs, support for
agricultural, biofuels production, and other industries that require process heat and cost
reductions for existing utility customers through better utilization of existing grid assets. Antora
has late stage developments in Texas including an interconnection filing in Batch Zero while
Antora has recently energized a project that would be classified as a Large Load within
Midcontinent Iso territory in Big Stone, South Dakota that operates under a coincident peak
based cost structure.

Transmission is sized for coincident peak demand, and peak therefore drives nearly all
incremental transmission investment.3 Highly flexible loads that can be curtailed as needed do
not contribute to peak transmission needs. Off-peak consumption uses existing spare capacity at
near-zero marginal cost. Because Antora's facilities are designed to avoid coincident peaks and
have low load factors, are price sensitive and highly flexible, they avoid coincident peaks, charge
only when the grid has spare capacity, and when low-value hours of generation are available.
That means Antora's thermal storage projects "fill valleys" of demand and should not be
confused with additional on-peak load combined with low utilization of grid assets.

A load that verifiably avoids coincident peaks - and, under the alternative proposed in Section
IV below, is contractually barred from consuming at peak - adds no peak-driven transmission
investment, so planners can rely on peak avoidance rather than build for it. Antora's projects are
different from other Demand Response or strategically peak avoidant loads that may decide peak

II. Demand Charges Untethered from Coincident Peak Eliminate the Market Signal for
Flexibility

Under the PFP, the MBD equals the greater of (A) the customer's contracted peak demand, (B)
its highest non-coincident peak ("NCP") demand in the preceding year, or (C) its actual
coincident-peak demand; the MBD applies when capacity is available and for a period of no less
than 20 years.8 Billing commences at the level of available service, irrespective of whether the
large-load customer has energized or is fully using its available capacity.9

Collectively, these design features convert every flexible load into a firm load for billing purposes
on day one. This sends poor, inefficient investment signals and poor operation signals,
discouraging the beneficial load behaviors described in Section II that lower transmission costs
for everyone else while utilities will be forced to build transmission based on a contracted peak.
Without changes, the MBD risks eliminating the investment opportunity in Texas for large highly
flexible loads, like Antora's thermal storage, that can reduce and share fairly allocated grid costs.


    1. Non-Coincident Peak Demand charges are a blunt instrument that destroys the
       value of flexibility. A load that pays the same transmission charge whether it consumes at
       system peak or only in the deepest off-peak valleys of demand has no remaining signal to
       curtail, shift, or respond transmission costs. The central economic case for building
       flexibility into a facility - storage, curtailment capability, price-responsive scheduling -
       is transmission cost causation and subsequent cost allocation. Charges on contracted or
       non-coincident demand substantially reduce or eliminate the rationale for investing in
       flexibility and encourage all customers to consume like a firm load. Overpricing off-peak
       network use deters investment in flexible loads that raise system utilization and steers
       investment toward full-firm configurations that increase total system costs - causing an
       unnecessarily overbuilt and expensive system.

         In Antora's case the flexibility value destruction is even more severe: Antora's industrial
         heat storage projects are designed to charge at -3 times their discharge rate to maximize
         their ability to absorb low value hours of electricity generation and completely avoid high
         cost (and peak) hours. Under the MBD, that means a triple penalty for investment that

III. Distinguishing Committed Industrial Flexibility

In sections IV and V below, we recommend limited alternatives to the MBD, should the
commission determine a coincident peak based charge is insufficient. The Section VI narrow
alternative and the Section VII hybrid proposal sorts loads by verifiable, enforceable
commitments rather than industry label - any load unwilling to accept binding curtailment pays
the default; eligibility is earned by performance, not granted by industry classification. In this
section we differentiate between certifiable highly flexible loads and load that may vary their
demand response behavior subject to economic conditions.

    1. Physical versus financial flexibility. Antora's flexibility is embedded in the asset:
       thermal storage decouples charging from delivery, so peak avoidance is the permanent
       design basis and can be committed contractually for the life of the facility. Antora's
       thermal storage is also designed for multi-day operation, allowing it to accept curtailment
       across extended periods of grid stress without interrupting service to its industrial hosts.
       This means nearly limitless flexibility to support grid reliability and lower grid costs,
       where economic demand response, unless tied to enforceable commitments, floats with
       opportunity costs - flexibility that cannot be committed and can evaporate when margins
        rise.
    2. Anchored, long-lived assets. Antora facilities are capital-intensive infrastructure serving
       long standing and fixed Texas industrial plants under long-term offtake contracts.
       Containerized mining loads can relocate to the next cheapest grid, which is precisely the
       stranded-infrastructure risk this rule targets.
    3. Wider economic development. Thermal storage loads directly support the Texas
       manufacturing and industrial base -jobs, local tax base, and onshoring of industrial
       capacity - rather than exporting a purely digital or financial product.
    4. Security and resilience for Texas industry. Stored energy provides firm, continuous
       heat and power to industrial hosts and the grid even while the electric load curtails during
       grid stress - the load steps off the grid when prices rise, including during peaks, instead
       of competing with residential customers, while Texas industry keeps running. Stable,
       low-cost industrial energy, and the resiliency of decoupling industrial supply from grid
       conditions, are competitiveness and security assets for the state.
    5. Reliability contribution. Committed flexible/curtailable loads function as dispatchable
       demand reduction during scarcity, complementing SB 6's emergency curtailment
       framework for large loads under PURA §37.056116 rather than straining it.

 EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Antora is a thermal energy storage developer whose facilities charge flexibly during off-peak
hours to deliver firm industrial heat and power; cost allocation that rewards this behavior lowers
costs for all ratepayers while supporting new industrial investment in Texas. Antora Energy
respectfully submits these comments on the Commission's Proposal for Publication ("PFP") in
Project No. 58000 to raise a targeted, remediable concern: as drafted, the proposed minimum
billing demand ("MBD") charges flexible, curtailable large loads - including thermal energy
storage - for transmission capacity based on contracted or non-coincident peak demand, rather
than the coincident peak demand that actually drives transmission investment. That design
eliminates the price signal that rewards loads for consuming during off-peak, low-cost hours and
avoiding system peaks, and it does so precisely for facilities - like Antora's - that are
engineered to fill demand valleys, absorb low value hours of generation that would otherwise be
curtailed, and impose little to no incremental transmission cost.

Antora requests that the Commission:

           1. Base transmission billing and class allocation on actual coincident-peak demand,
              consistent with the cost-causation principle underlying 16 TAC §25.192 and
              PURA Chapter 36;
           2. Reject demand charges keyed to contracted or non-coincident peak demand,
              which cross-subsidize peak consumption and eliminate the incentive for
              investment in flexible load;
           3. If a demand-based minimum is retained, adopt either (a) a behavioral alternative
              billing framework under which loads earn coincident-peak-only billing by
              accepting binding, tariffed curtailment obligations (Section III below), or (b) an
              85/15 hybrid recovery mechanism combining a coincident-peak demand charge
              with a small unavoidable volumetric charge (Section IV below);
                   a. Recover any residual, non-coincident-peak-driven cost share on an energy
                       ($/MWh) basis rather than a non-coincident-peak basis.

           4. Exclude load served entirely within a private use network from the MBD, billing
              determinants, and the ALLOC class allocator, since such load never uses the
              shared transmission network; and
           5. Recover any residual, non-coincident-peak-driven cost share on an energy
              ($/MWh) basis rather than a non-coincident-peak basis.

Antora offers to provide operational data and to participate in any workshop or cost-benefit
analysis the Commission convenes on flexible-load transmission billing.
